comment: Orbital elements (epoch 2000.0) per Paul Schlyter's method. Angles in degrees, rates in deg/day, distances in AU. Moon perturbation terms live in solarsystem.js; the Sun follows Earth's mirrored orbit, so no Sun entry here.

bodies.name: Mercury
facts: A Mercurian day (sunrise to sunrise) lasts 176 Earth days — twice its 88-day year.
Temperatures swing from 430°C in daylight to −180°C at night.
Despite being closest to the Sun, it is not the hottest planet — that's Venus.
Its huge iron core makes it the second-densest planet.

bodies.name: Venus
facts: Venus spins backwards, and so slowly that its day is longer than its year.
Its runaway greenhouse keeps the surface near 465°C — hot enough to melt lead.
Surface pressure is 92 times Earth's, like being 900 m underwater.
It is the brightest planet in our sky, glowing steadily because of its thick cloud deck.

bodies.name: Mars
facts: Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest volcano in the Solar System — nearly 3× Everest.
Mars has the largest canyon system, Valles Marineris, over 4,000 km long.
Its red color comes from iron oxide — literally rust — dust.
It has two tiny moons, Phobos and Deimos, likely captured asteroids.

bodies.name: Jupiter
facts: Jupiter outweighs all the other planets combined — 2.5 times over.
The Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has raged for centuries.
It has 95 known moons, including Ganymede, bigger than Mercury.
Its day is the shortest of any planet: under 10 hours.

bodies.name: Saturn
facts: Saturn is the least dense planet — it would float in water.
Its rings are mostly water ice, and may be younger than the dinosaurs.
Its moon Titan has rivers and lakes of liquid methane.
A hexagonal jet stream circles its north pole — a hexagon wider than two Earths.

bodies.name: Uranus
facts: Uranus rolls on its side, tilted 98° — possibly knocked over by an ancient impact.
Each pole gets 42 years of sunlight, then 42 years of darkness.
It is the coldest planet, dipping below −220°C.
It was the first planet discovered with a telescope, by William Herschel in 1781.

bodies.name: Neptune
facts: Neptune was found by mathematics before it was seen — predicted from Uranus's wobble.
It has the fastest winds in the Solar System, over 2,000 km/h.
One Neptunian year lasts 165 Earth years; it has completed one orbit since discovery in 1846.
Its moon Triton orbits backwards and erupts nitrogen geysers.

sunFacts: It holds 99.86% of the Solar System's mass.
About 1.3 million Earths would fit inside it.
Light from its surface takes about 8.3 minutes to reach Earth.
It converts about 4 million tons of matter into energy every second.
moonFacts: It always shows us the same face — its rotation matches its orbit.
It drifts about 3.8 cm farther from Earth every year.
Moonlight is reflected sunlight; the Moon makes no light of its own.
Twelve people have walked on it, all between 1969 and 1972.
